document.title: Query Processing and Optimization in Search Engines
document.section: Query processing is the set of steps a search engine takes to transform a raw user query into a ranked list of relevant documents. Efficient query processing is critical for search engines handling millions of queries per second.

Query parsing involves tokenizing the input text, removing stop words, applying stemming or lemmatization, and identifying operators such as AND OR NOT and phrase quotes. The parsed query is then mapped to index terms for posting list lookup.

section.name: query_types
section.type: Single or multiple unstructured keywords. The most common form of web search query.
Terms enclosed in quotes requiring exact adjacency in the document. Processed using positional inverted indexes.
Explicit logical operators AND OR NOT for precise document filtering without ranking.
Terms must appear within a specified word distance. Useful for finding related concepts near each other.
Queries with asterisk or question mark wildcards matched against permuterm or k-gram indexes.

document.section: Query optimization techniques include index compression using gamma and delta encoding, skipping in postings list traversal, document-at-a-time versus term-at-a-time evaluation, early termination using WAND and BMW algorithms, and caching frequent query results. These optimizations enable sub-millisecond response times for typical web queries.

Spell correction uses edit distance algorithms like Levenshtein distance and k-gram jaccard similarity to suggest alternative query terms when no or few results are found. Phonetic algorithms like Soundex handle phonetic misspellings.

Automatic query expansion adds synonyms and related terms using thesauri, WordNet, or pseudo-relevance feedback. Global analysis uses the entire corpus while local analysis uses top-ranked documents to expand the query. Query expansion improves recall at the risk of reducing precision if irrelevant terms are added.
